This is a really important story. It's a rewriting of two different stories: the Garden of Eden, where God told Adam and Eve not to eat the fruit, and Augustine's Confessions. In Augustine's story, when he was young, he and his friends stole pears from a tree because they recognized it wasn't about hunger or taste but their own evil nature.

JF Frank criticizes this story, saying that what God wants is for humans to break man-made rules in order to be more wealthy. He emphasizes that God cares about creativity and exploration, as long as these actions don't involve killing or hurting others. JF Frank believes we should gain power through trickery and deception without worrying about morality or convention.

Jacob Frank, a Cabalist, teaches that reality is just a hallucination created by our imagination. Laws and taboos are all constructs made up by humans; if everyone believes in them but they don't truly exist, you can use this belief to your advantage. He argues that breaking these laws will make you powerful.

The text then references a passage comparing Jews negatively, suggesting they are like snakes and crocodiles due to their lack of love and constant contention. It mentions a riddle about lifting something no one else can—convention or social norms—and states that once you see the truth, you become God-like.

Frank's followers should think for themselves and challenge these conventions, as the rabbis who enforce them are also human and not infallible.
